resources.string: Your private prayer companion. Free, always.
SajdaTime works out your prayer times and the Qibla from a rough idea of where you are.

To work out the right prayer times and Qibla direction for where you are.\n\nWe only check your approximate location while the app is open. The times are worked out on your phone and we never receive your location. To show your town\'s name, the app asks your phone\'s own place lookup, which on most phones is answered over the internet by Google.
We could not get a fix. Check that location is turned on, or type where you are below.

Type where you are instead. The name is looked up by your phone\'s own place lookup, which on most phones asks Google over the internet. If that cannot answer, just the name you typed is sent once to a free lookup service. After that, everything is worked out on your phone.
The name you type is looked up over the internet. After that, everything is worked out on your phone.

If you type a place instead, the name is looked up by your phone\'s own place lookup, which on most phones asks Google over the internet. If that cannot answer, just the name you typed is sent once to a free lookup service. After that, everything is worked out on your phone.
For example: Karachi, London, Makkah, New York

This sets how your prayer times are worked out. You can change it whenever you like.
Muslim World League times by default
This only changes the Asr time. Hanafi mosques begin Asr later. Shafi\'i, Maliki and Hanbali use the standard time. Not sure? Keep Shafi\'i for the standard time. You can change it later in Settings.
Later Asr, when a shadow is twice the object\'s length
Standard Asr, when a shadow equals the object\'s length

Mosques measure the dawn and evening twilight differently, so Fajr and Isha can differ by some minutes from one method to another, and by over an hour in the far north. If your mosque\'s times differ from the app, choosing its method here is usually the fix. Not sure? Keep the first option. You can change this any time in Settings.
Look right? You can change any of this later in Settings.

SajdaTime is a helper, not a religious authority.

These times are not given to me by a mosque, a scholar, or any authority. Your phone works them out from the position of the sun, using calculation methods that Islamic authorities and scholars have published. I am not a Mufti, Aalim, or an expert in fiqh, and this app was built with the help of artificial intelligence. Software can carry faults, a phone can hold the wrong location or the wrong clock, a phone saving its battery can delay an alert, and I can simply be wrong.

So please take what you see here as a calculation and not a ruling. Where SajdaTime and your mosque disagree, follow your mosque. If a time or a direction looks off to you, or you are unsure, ask them or someone else qualified to advise you. The app is free and is given as it is, with no warranty and no promise of accuracy, so where being exact matters to you, please do not rely on it alone.

If you use the watch, please treat it as a convenience rather than the last word. A watch has a smaller compass and a poorer view of the sky than a phone, and it may be working from a location your phone found some time ago. For the Qibla especially, your phone is the more accurate of the two. When it matters, check there.

Mosques do not all agree on when a prayer starts. Isha varies the most. In Britain and further north the gap between one method and another can be over an hour, because scholars measure the fading of the twilight differently. I cannot settle that, and the app does not try to. If the times here do not match your mosque, ask them which method they use and pick it in Settings, under Calculation method. If a few minutes still separate you after that, Match your mosque lets you adjust each prayer, and the date, by hand. Where a difference remains, follow your mosque.

One more thing. This app shows when a prayer becomes due. Your mosque then sets its own time for the congregation, usually a little later, so the board there and the times here will often differ. Neither is wrong.

And one request, if you would: please remember me, my family, and my parents in your duas.

SajdaTime is a helper, not a religious authority.

No mosque or scholar supplies these times. Your phone calculates them from the position of the sun. I am not a Mufti or Aalim, and the app was built with the help of artificial intelligence, so a software fault, a wrong location or a wrong clock can make a time wrong.

Where SajdaTime and your mosque disagree, follow your mosque. The app is free and given as it is, with no warranty.
Fajr and Isha can differ by an hour or more here.
This app shows when each prayer becomes due. Your mosque usually holds the congregation a little later, so its board and these times will often differ by some minutes. Neither is wrong.
Fajr and Isha depend on how the twilight is measured, and mosques measure it differently. If yours differs by more than a few minutes, choose the method it follows.
Asr depends on the school of thought. Hanafi mosques begin Asr later than others, by up to an hour or more.
If a few minutes still separate you, nudge each prayer to match your mosque\'s printed times.
Where a difference remains, follow your mosque.

This far from the equator the sun does not always rise or set, so there is no true Fajr or Isha to calculate. These times are worked out from latitude %1$d° instead. Mosques here handle it in different ways, so ask yours what it follows.

On these days your alarms arrive as quiet notifications instead of ringing, because the app cannot vouch for the exact minute. Turn on “Ring on approximate days” in Settings if you would rather be woken anyway.
Set your location to see prayer times.
Your location is not set yet, so these times are for Makkah.

Prayer times and the Qibla both depend on where you are. Update this whenever you travel.\n\nTo protect your privacy the app only ever asks for your approximate position, so it may name a nearby town or the wider area rather than yours. That changes the times very little: ten miles is about a minute. If the name looks wrong to you, type where you are below.
We will make a PDF of your prayer times for %1$s. You can then save it, print it, or send it to someone.

Some of these times are approximate. This far north the sun does not always rise or set, so those days are worked out from latitude %1$d° instead. Ask your mosque what it follows.

The compass needs calibrating. Hold your phone and move it in a figure of eight a few times.
This phone has no compass, so we can give you the angle but cannot point the way.
The reading may wander a little. Move away from metal, magnets and speakers for a steadier result.

Mosques measure the twilight differently, and that mainly moves Fajr and Isha. The further north you live, the bigger the gap. If these times do not match your mosque, ask them which method they use and pick it here.
Notification: plays the notification sound and vibrates. Alarm: plays the alarm sound at alarm volume and vibrates. Choose each sound in Settings, just below Prayer alerts.

Plays when a prayer notification arrives, at your notification volume. Your phone\'s silent, vibrate and Do Not Disturb settings still apply. Pulling down your notifications or swiping the notification away stops the sound.
Plays for prayers set to Alarm, at your alarm volume.
Plays even when your phone is on silent or Do Not Disturb. Off: notification and vibration only.
Allow sound during Do Not Disturb
Without this, your alarm stays silent when the phone is on Do Not Disturb.
A silent notification with the next prayer and the time left
Prayer alerts can arrive an hour late.
Without it, prayer alerts can arrive an hour or more late, and on some phones Fajr may not arrive at all.

Android does not let apps set alerts for an exact minute unless you say so. Without it your phone can hold prayer alerts back by an hour or more, and on some phones an overnight alert like Fajr may not arrive at all. You can also do this later from Settings.
A helper, not a religious authority. Tap to read.
Times are worked out on this phone, and we never receive your location. No accounts and no ads. Usage counts stay off unless you turn them on.

SajdaTime is free and has no ads. If you say yes, it sends a few usage counts to Google Analytics so the app can be improved. They are tied to a random ID, not your name, and may be processed outside the UK. Detailed records are kept for 14 months.

Using a prayer app can say something about your faith, so this is your choice, and nothing changes in the app if you say no. SajdaTime never sends your GPS position or your prayer settings.

Until you choose yes, nothing is sent. You can switch it off in Settings at any time. The person responsible is Ali Imran Khan, who made the app.
Choose the language of the app
What is sent if you say yes

• Which main screen you open: Times, Qibla or Settings
• Which setup steps you reach
• Whether you allow notifications, location and exact alarms (a yes or no each, never the location itself)
• How often and for how long the app is open
• Your phone model, Android version, app version and language
• When you first opened the app, and how you found the app (for example a link on Google Play)
• Your approximate area, which Google works out from your internet connection

• Your GPS position or coordinates
• The place you type
• Your sect, your prayer calculation setting, your calculation method and your alert settings
• Anything you have typed
The full privacy policy is in English.
Tell the developer what helps or what is wrong. Opens your email.
Off unless you turn it on. Sent to Google with a random ID. Turning it on first shows exactly what is sent.

If your mosque prints a different time, nudge it here, or set the time its board shows. Try the calculation method first. That is usually the real difference, and this is for the few minutes left over.
%1$s: the time on your mosque\'s board
A gap of %1$d minutes or more is usually a different calculation method, or a mosque board that shows the congregation time, which is a little later. Try the method first.
The Islamic date here is calculated. If your mosque sights the moon locally, it can be a day either way. This also moves Ramadan and Eid.
When the sun does not rise or set, times are worked out from a lower latitude. Alarms stay quiet on those days unless you turn this on.
On this calendar today is the last day of Ramadan. Your mosque will announce Eid.
SajdaTime shows Fajr and Maghrib as calculated for your location and uses them as the end of suhoor and the time of iftar.
Many timetables print an imsak time a few minutes before Fajr as a precaution, and some mosques begin Fajr earlier than this calculation. SajdaTime does not add a margin.
Where your mosque\'s timetable differs, follow your mosque.

The Islamic date here follows the Umm al-Qura calendar. If your mosque began Ramadan on a different day, shift the Islamic date in Settings. That also moves the day count, the suhoor reminder and the Umm al-Qura Isha rule.
You can show it again in Settings.
Many mosques announce their own start after sighting the moon, often a day later. If yours differs, shift the Islamic date. That also moves the suhoor reminder and the Umm al-Qura Isha rule.
Did your mosque begin Ramadan on a different day?

Every day of the month, with suhoor and iftar
Suhoor ends at Fajr. Iftar at Maghrib. Follow your mosque where its timetable differs.
A reminder before Fajr on the days of Ramadan, on the calendar SajdaTime is set to. As an alarm it uses the same sound as your prayer alerts.
A quiet notification a few minutes before each prayer you choose, so you have time to get ready.
